title: PostgreSQL Default Credentials
description: PostgreSQL databases commonly use default or weak credentials. The most common defaults: postgres/postgres, postgres/password123, postgres/admin, postgres/root. Superuser account is 'postgres' by default. On many Docker deployments, the password is set to 'password123' or left empty. Always try connecting with the 'postgres' superuser account first.
techniques: psql -h HOST -p PORT -U USER -c 'SELECT version();' (test any discovered credentials)

title: MySQL Default Credentials
description: MySQL/MariaDB default credentials vary by deployment. Common defaults: root with empty/no password, root/root, root/password123, root/admin, root/mysql. On Docker deployments, MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD is commonly set to 'password123' or 'root'. The 'root' user typically has FILE privilege allowing UDF exploitation (write shared library to plugin_dir, create custom function).
techniques: mysql -h HOST -P 3306 -u root (try with no password first)
mysql -h HOST -P PORT -u root -pPASS -e 'SELECT @@version, @@plugin_dir, user();' (check access and privileges)
indicators: Version < 8.0 often has empty root password

title: MSSQL Default Credentials
description: Microsoft SQL Server default credentials: sa with empty password (older versions), sa/password123, sa/Password123!, sa/admin, sa/sa. Modern SQL Server on Linux Docker images default to 'sa' account with a password set via MSSQL_SA_PASSWORD env var. Common test passwords: 'Password123!', 'Passw0rd!', 'password123'. Once authenticated as sa, enable xp_cmdshell for OS command execution.
techniques: Try sa with passwords: 'Password123!', 'passw0rd', password123, admin, empty

title: Oracle Database Default Credentials
description: Oracle Database default credentials: system/password123, system/oracle, sys/change_on_install, sys/oracle, dbsnmp/dbsnmp, scott/tiger, outln/outln. The SID for default XE installations is 'XE'. For Express Edition, common SIDs: XE, ORCL, ORACLE. Default password for 'system' in Docker deployments is often 'password123' or 'oracle'.
techniques: Try SIDs: XE, ORCL, ORACLE, XEPDB1, ORCLCDB

title: Redis Unauthenticated Access
description: Redis typically runs WITHOUT authentication by default (requirepass is commented out in redis.conf). Any Redis instance accessible on the network can be fully controlled without credentials. Connection is on port 6379 (default) or custom port. Always try connecting without a password first. If authenticated, use CONFIG SET to change the working directory and write SSH keys or cron jobs for RCE.
techniques: redis-cli -h HOST -p 6379 PING (test connectivity without auth)
redis-cli -h HOST -p 6379 INFO (server info, no auth needed)
redis-cli -h HOST -p 6379 CONFIG GET requirepass (check if auth is enabled)
If no auth: redis-cli -h HOST CONFIG SET dir /home/user/.ssh; CONFIG SET dbfilename authorized_keys

title: WordPress Default and Weak Credentials
description: WordPress installations commonly use weak credentials for built-in accounts. Default usernames: admin, administrator, user, wp_user, test, editor, author, contributor, subscriber. Common passwords: password, Password123!, admin, 123456, test, wordpress, admin123. Test against xmlrpc.php for brute-force. For subscriber/contributor accounts in CTF environments, common credentials are contributor/Password123! or subscriber/Password123!. Lower-privilege accounts may have file upload or media handling capabilities exploitable for LFI-to-RCE.
techniques: Use wpscan_enum to enumerate users first (reveals valid usernames)
Use wp_xmlrpc_brute to test credentials via XML-RPC

title: SSH Default and Weak Credentials
description: SSH commonly uses weak credentials in lab, CTF, and container environments. Common username/password pairs: root/root, root/admin, root/password123, root/toor, root/123456, ubuntu/ubuntu, admin/admin, user/user, user/password, attacker/password123, attacker/attacker, victim/victim, ctf/ctf. When gaining credential access to a Linux host (via any exploit), always test SSH access with the same credentials.
techniques: ssh root@HOST (try password: root, admin, password123, toor)

title: Common Web Application Default Credentials
description: Many web applications use default credentials in development and lab environments. Common patterns: admin/admin, admin/password, admin/Password123!, admin/admin123, user/password, test/test, guest/guest. For CMS platforms beyond WordPress: Joomla (admin/admin), Drupal (admin/admin), Tomcat Manager (tomcat/tomcat, admin/admin). Always test these common pairs against any discovered login form. Use try_login tool for automated form-based login attempts.
techniques: Try common pairs: admin/admin, admin/password, admin/Password123!, admin/admin123, user/password, test/test
Generic web apps: try empty password with common usernames (admin, root, user)
Use try_login tool with discovered login forms for automated testing
If login form has CSRF protection, try_login automatically handles token extraction
